title: The 2026 AI Index Report - Economy chapter
date_evidence: The Stanford AI Index 2026 was published April 13, 2026, by Stanford's Human-Centered AI Institute (HAI).
key_claim: Global corporate AI investment more than doubled in 2025; AI company revenue is rising at historically fast rates, but compute costs and infrastructure spending are also reaching record levels (Google reported more than $150 billion in annual capex in 2025); organizational adoption rose to 88% but AI agent deployment was in the single digits across nearly all business functions.
notes: Tier 2 academic data compilation. Anchors the consensus (investment doubling, prices falling) while flagging compute costs at record levels and agent adoption still single-digit.

title: AI and the euro area economy - keynote speech by Philip R. Lane
key_claim: AI is already driving a substantial surge in capital expenditure among leading technology firms, particularly in data centre infrastructure, semiconductors and energy systems; estimates of the macroeconomic impact of AI range from modest to transformative, and the productivity J-curve implies aggregate gains materialise only after a substantial lag.
notes: Tier 1 central-bank primary source. Used for the AI capex surge and the dispersion / productivity-lag framing.

title: Global Economic and Financial Implications of Artificial Intelligence: Lessons from a Scenario-Planning Exercise (IMF Note 2026/002)
date_evidence: NOTE/2026/002 ... Washington, DC: International Monetary Fund, 2026. | Apr. 2026. | Note/2026/XXX.
key_claim: Although access costs continue to decline, with inference prices for certain frontier models dropping by over 99 percent, participants emphasised that adoption remains constrained by institutional and organizational frictions rather than by the price of frontier capability.
verbatim_quote: inference prices for certain frontier models dropping by over 99 percent
notes: Tier 1 multilateral primary research. Directly anchors the consensus (token prices collapsing >99%) and the framing that the binding constraint is adoption/frictions, not unit price.

title: Unlocking agentic value: a new investment discipline for the agentic era (Total Cost of Agents series)
key_claim: Agentic AI shifts enterprise AI from fixed software/labour costs to variable compute use: a customer-service chat that once cost $0.04 may now involve tool retrieval, planning and subagents that turn it into a $1.20 orchestration (about 30x higher); agentic workflows can consume hundreds of thousands of tokens in a single session; providers are shifting from subscription to consumption-based pricing, ending vendor-subsidised pricing; EY cites Gartner that more than 40% of agentic AI projects will be cancelled by end-2027 due to escalating costs, unclear value or inadequate controls.
verbatim_quote: a chat that once cost $0.04 may now involve tool retrieval, planning and subagents that turn it into a $1.20 orchestration
notes: Tier 2 major-consultancy analysis. Core quantification anchor for per-task token escalation and the shift to Agent FinOps / consumption pricing. The 40% cancellation figure is EY citing Gartner; attributed to EY at point of use.

title: Uber burned through its entire 2026 AI budget in four months. Now its COO is questioning whether it's worth it
key_claim: Uber burned through its entire 2026 AI coding-tools budget in four months; a Gartner study found inference on sophisticated models will cost 90% less by 2030 than in 2025, but cheaper tokens won't translate to cheaper enterprise AI because agentic models require far more tokens per task and providers won't fully pass through lower costs; Gartner separately forecasts AI agent software spending will reach nearly $207 billion in 2026, up more than 139% from $86.4 billion in 2025; Anthropic moved from a flat fee to usage-based per-token pricing.
notes: Tier 3 quality journalism. Concrete enterprise example (Uber) plus the Gartner $207bn agent-spend and 90%-by-2030 figures (attributed to Gartner via Fortune; Gartner's own release predates the window).

title: How persistent is the inference cost burden?
date_evidence: meta-pagefind:date: Mon Feb 16 2026 00:00:00 GMT+0000 ... Newsletter Feb. 16, 2026
key_claim: Although per-use inference costs cannot be amortised like training costs and can be significant in the short run, the dollar cost to reach a given capability level falls rapidly - roughly a 5-10x reduction per year - so the inference cost burden is more transient than it appears from looking only at frontier models at launch.
notes: Tier 2 research institute. Structural anchor (3-6m band) and the principal sourced counter-argument: cost-to-fixed-capability falls ~5-10x/yr.

title: 2026 State of AI: Bi-Annual Snapshot - The Execution Era of AI
date_evidence: ICONIQ Capital released their January 2026 'State of AI: Bi-Annual Snapshot' report, surveying approximately 300 executives at software companies building AI products.
key_claim: Across ~300 AI product leaders, gross margins on AI products are expected to keep improving, reaching about 52% on average in 2026 (up from 41% in 2024 and 45% in 2025) but well below the 80%+ typical of mature SaaS; cost ranks as the second model-selection criterion, builders now use ~3.1 model providers on average, and many route most workloads to smaller or fine-tuned models, escalating only high-complexity tasks to frontier models.
verbatim_quote: the companies surveyed expect gross margins to continue improving, reaching ~52% on average in 2026
notes: Tier 4 vendor survey, used as directional corroboration only. Structural anchor (3-6m band) for the AI-native gross-margin trajectory and multi-model cost-routing behaviour.
